932.title: The Maharaja close
932.hook: forty years of a Punjab kingdom, from Lahore's open gate to the samadhi
932.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign as the time of a Sikh kingdom in the Punjab, and tell its story from his taking of Lahore to his death, and the troubles that followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach, and your line, pride and honesty. Today, the story of the Maharaja comes to its close.

Lay two pictures side by side. In the first, a young chief with one eye rides through a gate of Lahore that someone inside has opened for him. In the second, a pale building with a gilded dome stands by the same city's Fort, holding his ashes. Everything in this part of the path happened between those two pictures. Histories count about forty years from the day he took Lahore to the day he died.
screen: `A GATE OPENED IN LAHORE.` → `A SAMADHI BY THE FORT.` → `EVERYTHING IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: A boy born in Gujranwala, scarred by smallpox and blind in one eye, led his misl young, with help around him. Lahore opened its gate to him. He took the title of Maharaja, but ruled as the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name. Look at what he built: gold on the Harmandir, a river line on the Sutlej he chose to keep, an army drilled in new ways by officers from many lands, Hari Singh Nalwa on the frontier, Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar joining the kingdom, the Koh-i-Noor on his arm, a court of many faiths, painters at work, gifts to Patna and Nanded, and a reputation for rarely ordering death. And Maharani Jind Kaur, the youngest queen, whose hardest days are still ahead. Then what he couldn't hold. He bowed at the Akal Takht and accepted its rebuke, so even he answered to something above the throne. But he left no settled way to hand on what he'd built. After he died, the kingdom came apart in the hands of rivals: two heirs lost, Sher Singh killed, a child on the throne, the army louder than the court. A kingdom so much one man's work was fragile without him. Forty years is a single working life: long enough to change the map, short enough that people who saw it begin could see it end. That's the sorrow in this story, and the honesty too. Some things are great and brief at once. Tomorrow a new part of the path begins, and it's harder: war with the British.

933.title: War with the British, 1845
933.hook: the Khalsa army crosses the Sutlej, and battles are fought at Mudki and Ferozeshah
933.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the opening battles of the war with the British, including Mudki and Ferozeshah, as a time of great courage by the Khalsa soldiers and of failure by some of their commanders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarkar-e-Khalsa, and your line, forty years. Today a new part of the path begins: loss and exile.

The Sutlej again. This is the river Ranjit Singh chose as a border with the British, and kept. On one bank, the Punjab. On the other, British India, where new regiments and guns have been arriving at the river towns. Now, on a winter's day, the Khalsa army is crossing that river with its guns and horses. The line the old Maharaja held for so long is being stepped over.
screen: `THE SUTLEJ, THE OLD BORDER.` → `BRITISH TROOPS AT THE RIVER TOWNS.` → `THE KHALSA ARMY CROSSES.`

segments.voice: Histories tell how the war came from more than one side. The British had been gathering troops near the Sutlej, and in Lahore that looked like a threat. The Khalsa army, proud and restless, was ready to fight. And Cunningham, the British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, suggests some leaders at the court were glad to send the army against the British, hoping it would be broken. Fear, pride and plotting, all at once. The opening battle was fought near a village called Mudki, late in the day, in dust and failing light, and the British held the field. Days later came a fiercer fight around the Sikh camp at Ferozeshah. The Khalsa soldiers fought hard behind their guns, and British accounts admit how close their own army came to disaster. But the Sikh army's commanders, Lal Singh and Tej Singh, made choices in those days that Sikh memory still questions, and the chance was lost. More of that tomorrow. In a verse of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Ninth Guru, the wise one is described as frightening no one and afraid of no one. That's not a battle plan. It's a way to stand inside a storm without losing your center: not ruled by fear, and not ruling others by it. The soldiers at Ferozeshah showed the fearless half. Some at the court that sent them, as Cunningham tells it, were ruled by fear of their own army.

934.title: Sobraon, 1846
934.hook: the Sikh army is defeated on the Sutlej, and Sikh memory holds that some of its own commanders betrayed it
934.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Sobraon with grief and honor, telling of Sham Singh Attariwala and the soldiers trapped at the river, and of commanders Sikh memory holds to have betrayed them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirbhau, and your line, war came. Today, the battle that ended that war.

An old general gets dressed for battle in white. Sikh tradition remembers him that way: Sham Singh Attariwala, gray-bearded, in white clothes, mounting his horse on the morning of the fight. In that telling, the white means he didn't expect to come home. Behind him the Sikh army is dug in along the bank of the Sutlej, with a bridge of boats at its back. In front of it, the British are forming up.
screen: `AN OLD GENERAL IN WHITE.` → `DUG IN ON THE SUTLEJ.` → `A BRIDGE OF BOATS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: At Sobraon the Khalsa army held strong earthworks on the river, and the British attacked them head on. The fighting was fierce, and for a time the Sikh lines held. Then the British broke through, and the Sikh soldiers were pushed back toward the river. Behind them stood the bridge of boats, their road home. Accounts say that Tej Singh, the commander, crossed back over it early, and that the bridge then broke, whether by the river, by the weight of men, or, as some tell it, by someone's order. With the bridge gone, soldiers were trapped against the water. Many died in the Sutlej that day, histories say, and few surrendered. The old general in white rode into the fighting and fell there. Sikh memory holds Sham Singh up beside the trapped soldiers as the honor of that day: men who were let down, and fought on anyway. Sikh memory also holds that the army's own commanders, Tej Singh and the minister Lal Singh, betrayed it, sending word to the British and leading their own soldiers badly on purpose. Cunningham, the British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, said much the same. Some historians weigh the evidence differently. But the hurt in the story isn't hard to understand. An enemy across the river is expected. A commander behind you who wants you to lose is something else.

935.title: The treaty and Kashmir
935.hook: Punjab loses land, and Kashmir is sold to Gulab Singh
935.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the treaties after the war with the British as a loss made on paper, in which the Punjab gave up land and Kashmir passed to Gulab Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sobraon, and your line, betrayal hurts most. Today the fighting is over, and the talking starts.

No guns this time. A table, papers, ink, men in good coats. On one side, British officials. On the other, ministers speaking for a boy Maharaja who isn't old enough to read what's being signed. The British army is camped at Lahore. Everyone at that table knows who won at Sobraon. What's left is to write down what it will cost. Land the Khalsa held is about to change hands without a shot.
screen: `A TABLE, PAPERS AND INK.` → `A BOY MAHARAJA'S MINISTERS.` → `WRITING DOWN THE COST.`

segments.voice: Under the treaty of Lahore, the kingdom gave up the fertile country between the Beas and the Sutlej rivers. The old river line Ranjit Singh had kept was pushed back into the heart of the Punjab. The Khalsa army was cut down in size, and British troops stayed in Lahore. The British also demanded a large payment for the cost of the war. The treasury in Lahore couldn't meet it, so in place of the money, the British took Kashmir and the hill country around it. Then, in a second treaty at Amritsar, they sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh, the Dogra raja of Jammu. You met him at the court of many faiths, one of the Dogra brothers who served the Maharaja. In the war he had kept out of the fighting and acted as a go-between with the British. Now he became ruler of the valley the Sikh army had once climbed the passes to win. Kashmiris themselves were not asked. Sobraon was a battlefield, and Sikh memory honors the men who fell there. The treaty is remembered differently: as a loss made quietly, by signatures, with a raja who had served the court walking away as ruler of Kashmir. Some losses don't happen in the fight. They happen afterward, on paper, while the people affected aren't in the room.

936.title: The queen exiled
936.hook: Maharani Jind Kaur is separated from her son and sent away
936.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur, often called Rani Jindan, as a queen and mother who resisted British control and was separated from her son, Maharaja Duleep Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi, and your line, lost at a table. Today, the treaties reach the palace, and a mother.

A carriage waits in a palace courtyard in Lahore. The woman being taken to it has ruled the Punjab in her son's name. She has argued with ministers, faced down the army's councils, and spoken her mind to British officials. Now there are guards at her side, and the boy Maharaja is not coming with her. Somewhere in the palace behind her is her son. She is being sent away from him.
screen: `A CARRIAGE IN THE COURTYARD.` → `GUARDS AT HER SIDE.` → `HER SON STAYS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: After the war, a new agreement put the Punjab's government in the hands of a council of the court's chiefs and ministers, guided by a British Resident at Lahore. Maharani Jind Kaur, who had been regent, was set aside with a pension. Her son stayed on the throne, but she no longer had any say in how he was raised or how his kingdom was run. The British Resident came to believe she was plotting against the new order, and histories record accusations of a plot against British officials. She denied it, and the evidence is still argued over. Whatever the truth, the decision was made. She was taken from Lahore to the fort at Sheikhupura, some miles from the city, while the boy was kept at the palace. Later she was sent much further, out of the Punjab altogether. Histories record her protests, sharp and grieving, against being parted from her child. She asked for her son, and she wasn't given him. The boy, too young to choose anything, stayed among officials and tutors. Sikh memory calls her Rani Jindan and holds her up as a mother and a queen who would not bow quietly, even when she lost. Some British writers of the time painted her as dangerous; Sikh tellings remember her courage. Both views appear in the histories, and today's story belongs to her grief. A crown can be taken by treaty. Taking a child from his mother is a different kind of loss.

937.title: Multan rises, 1848
937.hook: a handover at a fortress city, an attack at the gate, and a revolt that leads to a second war
937.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the rising at Multan as the start of the second war with the British, a local quarrel over a handover that grew into a war for the whole Punjab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maharani: Jind Kaur, set aside and sent away, and your line, mother and son apart. Today, far from Lahore, a city catches fire.

Multan, a walled fortress city in the south of the Punjab. Its governor, Diwan Mulraj, has said he will step down. A new governor rides in to take his place, with British officers from Lahore beside him. They look over the fort. They receive the keys. Then they turn their horses toward the gate, and a soldier of the garrison steps forward with a spear. Within days the city is in open revolt, and before long the Punjab is at war again.
screen: `A FORTRESS CITY IN THE SOUTH.` → `THE KEYS ARE HANDED OVER.` → `A SPEAR AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: After the first war, officers of the East India Company sat close to the court at Lahore, with a heavy hand in its decisions. Mulraj had governed Multan for that court, and he was in a dispute with Lahore over the revenue the province owed. So he offered to resign, and a new governor came down with British officers to take charge. As the officers left the fort, men of the garrison set on them and wounded them. They took shelter outside the walls, and soon after they were killed there. Did Mulraj give the order? That has never been fully settled. Some histories say he planned the rising from the start. Others say his own soldiers struck first and he was swept along, unable or unwilling to turn back once blood was shed. Herbert Edwardes, a British officer who gathered local fighters and marched on Multan, wrote his own account, and even his story leaves room for doubt. Then the revolt spread. Other Sikh leaders, angry at a kingdom now run from outside, joined it, Sher Singh Attariwala among them. And the governor-general, Lord Dalhousie, chose not a local settlement but a second war. In the saloks of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, Farid tells the reader to answer evil with good, and not to let anger fill the mind. A spear at a gate is a small thing. At Multan, it set a whole country burning.

938.title: Chillianwala, 1849
938.hook: a battle in thick scrub near the Jhelum, fought into the dark, and a Sikh army that would not give way
938.howItsDone: Sikh histories and tellings remember Chillianwala as a battle where the Khalsa army stood its ground against the British, and the story is told with pride alongside the losses that followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan rose, and your line was the spark. Today, the fire it started reaches a field by a river.

Late afternoon, near the river Jhelum. The ground ahead is thick with thorny scrub, so dense a soldier can barely see the man beside him. Somewhere in it waits the Sikh army under Sher Singh Attariwala. The British commander, Lord Gough, had meant to wait for morning. Instead, with the light already going, he orders the attack. Regiments push into the thorns, and guns open up from places nobody can see.
screen: `THORNY SCRUB BY THE JHELUM.` → `THE LIGHT IS GOING.` → `GOUGH ORDERS THE ATTACK.`

segments.voice: The Sikh army had chosen its ground well: behind cover, guns ready. The scrub broke up the British lines. Units lost touch with each other, and some charged straight into fire they couldn't see until it hit them. The fighting was close and bloody. British accounts describe regiments cut up, guns lost, and men falling back in confusion. On the Sikh side, an army that had lost at Sobraon, and seen land lost at the treaty table, fought hard and gave little away. Night came down on a field nobody had clearly won. The British held part of the ground and claimed the day. The Sikh army drew back in good order, still an army, still ready to fight. In Britain the news landed as a shock, and a new commander was sent out to replace Gough. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a salok of Bhagat Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the helpless (some read it, for the faith), and who, even cut to pieces, never leaves the field. In Sikh tellings, Chillianwala is that kind of day: no throne won, nothing changed on the map, but an army that stood its ground. Look back at the week: a kingdom's close and the first war, Sobraon and the treaty, the queen sent away, the spark at Multan. Each day, something taken. Today, something kept.

segments.voice: Sit with both feet flat on the floor and feel the ground under them, then bring to mind one place where you usually give way when you'd rather not: a conversation where you go quiet, a habit that wins every evening, a pressure at work. You don't have to fight it now; just feel your feet, and picture yourself, next time, staying where you are for one breath longer. If you pray, let Waheguru be the word on each breath out.
